flashcards.front: What is the primary threat vector for Network Level Exploits?
flashcards.back_definition: Adversaries exploit switch ARP cache spoofing on switch port tables to bypass standard perimeter security controls.
flashcards.back_example: Example: Conflict: Duplicate IP 192.168.1.1 bound to mismatched MAC
flashcards.back_confusion: Don't confuse this threat with other layers (like physical breaches or certificate revocations) which target different assets.
flashcards.back_hook: Recall: switch ARP cache spoofing is the unlocked door; switch port tables is what the attacker wants to steal.

flashcards.front: How does the security team mitigate Network Level Exploits threats?
flashcards.back_definition: Deploying and enforcing Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI) directly hardens switch port tables and blocks unauthorized connections.
flashcards.back_example: Action: Update security configurations to require Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI).
flashcards.back_confusion: Don't confuse mitigation (actively blocking the exploit) with detection (simply logging or alerting the event).
flashcards.back_hook: Mitigation is the shield; detection is the security camera.

flashcards.front: How do analysts detect exploitation of Network Level Exploits?
flashcards.back_definition: By auditing event data and implementing logic flags built to alert on duplicate IP mapping flags.
flashcards.back_example: Syslog trace: Conflict: Duplicate IP 192.168.1.1 bound to mismatched MAC
flashcards.back_confusion: Don't confuse signature-based detection (matching known strings) with anomaly-based detection (mapping dynamic standard deviations).
flashcards.back_hook: Detection is looking for the fingerprint left behind by the threat.
